Gauteng’s Deadly Air

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In the midst of the Covid 19 pandemic another silent killer continues to attack the people in and around Johannesburg... the deadly air that we breathe.

Unique Selling Point:
Take a look online at Johannesburg on IQAir's real time maps of air quality and pollution and the rankings of cities in terms of how hazardous their air is may give you a shock. Seeing Joburg up there with Indian and Chinese industrial cities is pretty scary. It is peculiar to compare the government’s SAAQIS map which uses the same data – indicators are less hazardous than the international IQAir indicators, apparently because South Africa standards are so low.

Earlier this year in February the government instigated a probe into unusually high levels of sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide in Mpumalanga and Gauteng and just past, this winter has seen dangerously high levels of pollution.

Johannesburg is not helped by its climate or geography. The city is surrounded by petrochemical industries and power generation industries. In winter the long weeks of static high pressure together with the heat of the concrete jungle trap the blanket of coal fired pollution for weeks on end.

But the air pollution in Johannesburg, Tshwane and surrounds does not only blow in from Mpumalanga’s coal burning power stations.

Summary:
In normal times poor air quality kills many people in Gauteng. In 2013, World Health Organization reported that air pollution killed almost 20,000 South Africans with the highest concentration of deadly pollution being in Tshwane and Johannesburg. These days the Covid 19 pandemic exacerbates these conditions for ill health, with the air pollution making Gauteng city dwellers more susceptible to the most acute effects of the coronavirus.

It is commonly understood that air pollution kills because of respiratory disease, but sulphur dioxide in the air reacts with other substances in the air forming small deadly particles of mixed chemicals that we breathe, causing not only lung disease, but heart disease and brain disease. This is because these PM2.5 particles are so small they get carried around our bodies within oxygen to all of our organs. The South African Air Quality Information Systems (SAAQIS) recorded twice the annual average of PM2.5 pollution at the end of July this year.

In early August levels of pollution exceeded the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) prompting health warnings especially in areas like Diepkloof and Jabavu advising residents to "reduce physical exertion, particularly outdoors."

So we're advised to live in well-ventilated areas because of Covid but to close all our windows to keep the hazardous pollution out.

What can be done to clean our skies while keeping the wheels of South Africa's economic hub turning?


Further information:
Picking up from John Webb’s story in 2019 which focused on Mpumalanga – this story on air pollution and its effects in South Africa, focuses on the air pollution in and around Johannesburg and the adverse health effects it produces.


Particular areas of exploration are:

- How bad is the air quality in Johannesburg and the surrounding areas and why is it so?


- What are the health effects attributed to air pollution?
We are setting up interviews with case studies who are suffering from bad health caused by the deadly air.


- Standards of data gathering and regulation in South Africa?

Professor Janine Wichmann of the University of Pretoria started her own data gathering unit at AP because of the low standards of data collection in SA. We are setting up a demo of this installation with Dr Adayemi.


- What are other pollutants out-with coal powered electricity generators are making an impact in Johannesburg, Tshwane and surrounds?

One main pollutant prevalent in Gauteng are the radioactive dust particles discarded in old goldmine dumps. Somewhat forgotten in the mix are domestic solid fuel burning (influenced by the ‘Energy Ladder’ effect) and the Illegal burning of waste (that’s not being collected) – both particulate matter. Not to mention the fumes that exude from road vehicles (Ozone)



- What actions should we be taking to tackle this issue in South Africa?

Why has there been little progress in reducing air pollution? The debate about alternatives to coal power stations, ‘Nuclear vs renewable’, with the jockeying for position, is akin to the endless postponements of state corruption trials.

Health and Environmental campaigners have opened the so-called Deadly Air Court Case.
The applicants, under the auspices of the Centre for Environmental Rights, are arguing in the High Court that the unsafe levels of ambient air pollution be declared a violation of section 24a of The Constitution, which states that "everyone has the right to an environment not harmful to their health or wellbeing". They want the court to order the minister to introduce strict and enforceable regulations to improve air quality.
Two environmental justice groups, groundWork and the Vukani Environmental Justice Movement are represented by the Centre for Environmental Rights in the case.
The respondents are the president, the minister of forestry, fisheries and the environment, the national air quality officer and the MECs for agriculture and rural development in Gauteng and Mpumalanga.
Heard on 17, 18 May this year, we await judgment.

Further to Eskom successfully applying to postpone compliance with Minimum Emission Standards for its existing power stations in 2014, in 27 March 2020 the government posted an Amendment to the National Environmental Management Air Quality Act 39 of 2004 – NEMAQA. This ostensibly means that existing power stations do not need to comply with emission standards until 2025, provided no further amendments are passed in the meantime.

WHO’s updated guidelines will be released on 22 September. The big debate within WHO is how do they apply these world guidelines in countries who are not necessarily geared to achieve these standards – then you’ve got Eskom who are one of the biggest contributors to pollution in Gauteng. In March this year Eskom said it will cost over R300 billion to upgrade its power plants to meet pollution standards. Eskom are reportedly trading off upgrading homes against its responsibility to meet air pollution standards. It installs electric stoves, gas stoves in homes, but the pollution to create the electricity and the gas is more toxic than what the stoves replace.


- What are PM2.5s and why are they so relevant to this matter?

In 2022 NASA are actually launching a satellite with new detectors onboard to study the distribution of these particles around the planet even further.



Interviews

Caradee Wright [ confirmed ]
Senior Specialist Scientist: South African Medical Research Council
Works in the field of air quality and finding ways to integrate public health into air quality management. Caradee also works in the broader field of environmental health, leading large epidemiological, cross-sectional community surveys to consider the impacts of environmental pollution on community health and develop appropriate interventions.
Can address the WHO recommendations amongst other issues

Mariette Liefferink [ confirmed ]
CEO: Federation for a Sustainable Environment
Will interview in situ at mine dumps in Krugersdorp. Campaigner highlighting the prevalence of radioactive dust in Joburg air.

Dr Adeyemi Adewale Adekunle [ confirmed ]
University of Pretoria (Air monitoring)
Will demonstrate the collection of air quality data at UP – can also reply to questions concerning PM2.5 particles

Press Release:


Gauteng - the hub of the South African economy, but at what cost? For years its citizens have paid the price for the deadly fallout of its air pollution. From radioactive fallout to sulphur dioxide emissions carried in tiny dust particles, many Gauteng residents are getting sick - under a toxic blanket of dirty air. In winter, some Gauteng cities rank amongst the top 20 most polluted in the world. What are the silent killers hiding in the murky layers of its sky? We take a toxic tour around the province to find out.

Script:


VO: The Gauteng skyline - characterised by spectacular sunsets in the winter months // - but these colourful displays mask a hidden danger.
Masa: In reality, the air we breathe is more hazardous than we imagine, with some of Gauteng’s cities ranked amongst the worst in the world when it comes to air pollution.
Timothy: There's this false perception though that if you're driving towards Johannesburg and Springs, away from Emalahleni and Middleburg where all the mines and power stations are, that you're leaving this pollution curtain behind you, and that once you're in Johannesburg, you're in a safe zone. But it cannot be further from the truth.
VO: Timothy Lloyd, an attorney at the Centre for Environmental Rights, is at the coalface of the war against pollution. He's seen from research that many of the province's citizens are feeling direct effects on their health.
Caitlin: We weren't able to breathe, we ended up coughing, having really bad headaches.
Vusi: At night I had this problem with my chest, coughing coughing
Vusi: So I went to the clinic. They told me that I've bronchitis, afterwards told me it's asthma.
VO: These people live in different parts of Gauteng, and yet their symptoms, varying from mild to severe, tell a similar story. // Investigating the adverse effects of air pollution linked to disease in South Africa is Dr Caradee Wright, of the Medical Research Council.
Caradee: Our work is to go into communities to understand the environmental risks posed not only from the outside air pollution, but also risks inside from them burning wood or coal, and then understand how it may be affecting their health, so that we can provide evidence for policy change.
Masa: Should this be at the top of our priorities?
Caradee: So according to the World Health Organisation, I think more than 7 million people around the world die every year prematurely because of exposure to air pollution.
VO: In March 2020, Cabinet approved amendments further limiting harmful sulphur dioxide emissions, derived mainly from burning fossil fuels, like coal. Heavy industry is delaying full compliance.
LINK: Sulphur dioxide in the air reacts with other substances forming small deadly particles of mixed chemicals that we breathe, causing not only lung disease, but heart and brain disease.
VO: Smaller in diameter than a strand of human hair, this life threatening particulate matter is categorised according to size, the main groups being PM10 and PM2.5. Studying these silent killers is Dr Adewale Adeyemi, of the University of Pretoria.
Dr Adeyemi: They are more or less invisible of interest is PM 2.5 because that PM 2.5 penetrates into our lung system. So that creates some health problems.
VO: So we set off into the murky shadow of Gauteng's dirty air, on the trail of some of these pollutants. Our first stop - Fourways, North of Johannesburg, where Caitlin Roos was a resident. Her health issues became so acute she had to leave the area.
Caitlin: We got respiratory infections, asthma attacks. My husband is very into fitness, he couldn't exercise because the smoke was too bad. Since moving out of the area in the last year all of my symptoms have disappeared.
VO: Our air quality is measured by the South African Air Quality Information System, SAAQIS. Daily levels can fluctuate dramatically, so activist Mduduzi Tshabalala of the Vaal Environmental Justice Project compares his live readings to the official data as part of his ongoing work. He joined us in Fourways from his hometown of Sebokeng.
Masa: What's happening in Sebokeng right now. What's the purple mean?
Mdu:When it is purple, it means it is beyond danger ,And when you look at the Pm 2.5 is 130 which is quite dangerous. But you look at the Pm 10 it's very, very, very dangerous.
Masa: Do you see this purple a lot?
Mdu: Yes, I took the device with me for like more than three months, and I was recording every week and it was bad.
VO: Following the ‘purple’ danger, we head south to Sebokeng, a region persistently cloaked in layers of toxic haze, and part of the Vaal Triangle Air-shed priority area. Resident Vusi Zulu, lived close to the industrial sector for about 10 years.
Vusi: There was a lot of smoke, dust. You can, even if you wash your car you can see in the morning, there's a this a a stof.
VO: But even now in his new home across the valley from the factories, he still battles with asthma.
Vusi: If starting raining of, the weather's changing of there's lot of smoke then I start getting the attacks.
VO: Escalating the crisis and recognised as one of the most polluted places in the world is the Highveld Priority area, covering parts of Gauteng and Mpumalanga.
Timothy: And that is largely due to the high concentration of coal fired power stations that we have in the area, along with coal mines and other industrial hotspots.
VO: It's been the focus of a landmark constitutional challenge since 2019.
Timothy: So in our Constitution, we have section 24 A of the Constitution, which is the right to an environment that is not harmful to one's health and well being.
VO: Dubbed the Deadly Air Case, it was spearheaded by the Centre for Environmental Rights on behalf of Groundwork andVukani Environmental Movement and heard at the High Court in May this year.
Timothy: The applicants are asking the court to force government to take further steps in the form of regulations, to reduce the levels of air pollution.
VO: Contaminants from this area also find their way into the city metros. But the main PM2.5 culprits come from vehicle emissions, burning of fossil fuels and local industry,
Caradee: Air Pollution will go up during winter months, when more people are burning coal and wood in Gauteng to heat water to cook food. And so you'll often see the the brown black layer of smog as you drive along the N1

VO: Dr Adeyemi gathers his data for Tshwane and its surrounds.
Dr Adeyemi: During that period, there are exceedances, That means is far above the standard of South African and WHO, like in my study, I think we have about 33 days that actually exceeded, the South Africa standard
VO: The difference between the South African standards for air quality and the WHO guidelines is staggering, as South Africa falls far short of the recommendations.// With Johannesburg peaking amongst the top 20 most polluted major cities in the world, July and August this year saw levels of pollution that prompted health warnings, advising some residents to "restrict activities and remain indoors"
Timothy: Medical studies indicate that there is actually no safe limit when it comes to particulate matter we ideally shouldn't be exposed to at all and we shouldn't be inhaling it at all.
VO: Heading off to the West Rand it gets worse, with more deadly ingredients in the mix.
LINK: Prevalent in Gauteng are dust particles circulating in the air from goldmine dumps. These particles are not only toxic but contain radioactive metals.
David Van Wyk: The dust contains uranium, it contains lead, it contains silica, it contains arsenic, all of them very bad poison.
VO: David Van Wyk, lead researcher with the Benchmarks Foundation, is measuring the levels of radiation with a Gieger Counter, here at Tudor Shaft Informal Settlement in Krugersdorp.
David Van Wyk: Normal levels of radiation is 0.10 And as we move closer to that mine dump, you will hear this device going beep beep beep faster and faster and faster. because the levels of uranium in the soil there is very high.
Masa: How’s it looking now?
David Van Wyk: 0.86
Masa: Oh my word so it shot up to 0.86?! And we’ve just moved a few metres
David Van Wyk: It's now almost nine times higher than what is the norm for background radiation, so the area here is quite radioactive. So these people here are very close to uranium and even if you don't see any shacks on the dump itself, the wind blows the dust into the community.
VO: Remnants of tailings or residue from the old mine lie unprotected here, with no warnings to keep people off the area. Cattle graze freely.
For more than a decade Carte Blanche has highlighted the significance of activist Mariette Liefferink’s work. As CEO of the Federation for a Sustainable Environment she has championed the plight of communities across the goldfields of the Witwatersrand, investigating the causal links between illness and mine waste.
Mariette: The research found that there is risk to human health because in this area since 1995, more than 600 persons stayed in shacks, without foundations on this dump area and adjacent to the dump area.
VO: Some of these previous residents came here to meet us, community leader David Pheto, wants their stories to be heard.
David: They were struggling with shortness of breath.. there's this boy, who was born in 2008, he started having a rash on his body, and it looked like skin is peeling off
Jack: When it's hot I get things that look like a rash. Water comes out.
Masa: So these are the marks it leaves?
Jack: Yes it leaves marks that don't go away.
Masa: So you say you're swollen?
Siphiwe: I was always working every day, but now I can't work because of this swelling and I can't do anything that I love to do because of this swelling.
VO: These accounts are anecdotal. And even though much research has been done, no epidemiological studies into the impact of radiation on the residents around South Africa's gold mines have been conducted.
Mariette: The eating of the tailings by especially pregnant women and young children. exposes the inhabitants to not only the physical dangers, but also of course to transgenerational impacts because of the radioactivity.
VO: However, the National Nuclear Regulator interprets its mandate narrowly, and only regulates where mining is taking place.
Mariette: There are 380 radioactive mine residue areas in Gauteng, upon which approximately 400,000 people are living.
VO: 270 of these facilities contain six hundred thousand tons of uranium.// And with the release of more stringent air quality guidelines by the WHO on the 22nd of September, how does South Africa even begin to meet standards that would alleviate the suffering of the hardest hit communities in pollution hotspots?
Caradee: It's a tricky challenge, meeting development needs, providing services to people, while at the same time trying to curb air pollution. We've got to get to one of the interim target level guideline values from the WHO, as best as we can.
VO: On request to participate in our programme, the Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development, declined to comment
Timothy: We've got a very advanced set of air quality laws in place. Publishing these air quality laws and plans, that's step one; step two is actually implementing these and making sure they're enforced. Without that second step, these laws that we have, aren't worth the paper that they're written on.

TEST ACCOUNT 10 January 2022 Press Release: Gauteng - the hub of the South African economy, but at what cost? For years its citizens have paid the price for the deadly fallout of its air pollution. From radioactive fallout to sulphur dioxide emissions carried in tiny dust particles, many Gauteng residents are getting sick - under a toxic blanket of dirty air. In winter, some Gauteng cities rank amongst the top 20 most polluted in the world. What are the silent killers hiding in the murky layers of its sky? We take a toxic tour around the province to find out. Script: VO: The Gauteng skyline - characterised by spectacular sunsets in the winter months // - but these colourful displays mask a hidden danger. Masa: In reality, the air we breathe is more hazardous than we imagine, with some of Gauteng’s cities ranked amongst the worst in the world when it comes to air pollution. Timothy: There's this false perception though that if you're driving towards Johannesburg and Springs, away from Emalahleni and Middleburg where all the mines and power stations are, that you're leaving this pollution curtain behind you, and that once you're in Johannesburg, you're in a safe zone. But it cannot be further from the truth. VO: Timothy Lloyd, an attorney at the Centre for Environmental Rights, is at the coalface of the war against pollution. He's seen from research that many of the province's citizens are feeling direct effects on their health. Caitlin: We weren't able to breathe, we ended up coughing, having really bad headaches. Vusi: At night I had this problem with my chest, coughing coughing Vusi: So I went to the clinic. They told me that I've bronchitis, afterwards told me it's asthma. VO: These people live in different parts of Gauteng, and yet their symptoms, varying from mild to severe, tell a similar story. // Investigating the adverse effects of air pollution linked to disease in South Africa is Dr Caradee Wright, of the Medical Research Council. Caradee: Our work is to go into communities to understand the environmental risks posed not only from the outside air pollution, but also risks inside from them burning wood or coal, and then understand how it may be affecting their health, so that we can provide evidence for policy change. Masa: Should this be at the top of our priorities? Caradee: So according to the World Health Organisation, I think more than 7 million people around the world die every year prematurely because of exposure to air pollution. VO: In March 2020, Cabinet approved amendments further limiting harmful sulphur dioxide emissions, derived mainly from burning fossil fuels, like coal. Heavy industry is delaying full compliance. LINK: Sulphur dioxide in the air reacts with other substances forming small deadly particles of mixed chemicals that we breathe, causing not only lung disease, but heart and brain disease. VO: Smaller in diameter than a strand of human hair, this life threatening particulate matter is categorised according to size, the main groups being PM10 and PM2.5. Studying these silent killers is Dr Adewale Adeyemi, of the University of Pretoria. Dr Adeyemi: They are more or less invisible of interest is PM 2.5 because that PM 2.5 penetrates into our lung system. So that creates some health problems. VO: So we set off into the murky shadow of Gauteng's dirty air, on the trail of some of these pollutants. Our first stop - Fourways, North of Johannesburg, where Caitlin Roos was a resident. Her health issues became so acute she had to leave the area. Caitlin: We got respiratory infections, asthma attacks. My husband is very into fitness, he couldn't exercise because the smoke was too bad. Since moving out of the area in the last year all of my symptoms have disappeared. VO: Our air quality is measured by the South African Air Quality Information System, SAAQIS. Daily levels can fluctuate dramatically, so activist Mduduzi Tshabalala of the Vaal Environmental Justice Project compares his live readings to the official data as part of his ongoing work. He joined us in Fourways from his hometown of Sebokeng. Masa: What's happening in Sebokeng right now. What's the purple mean? Mdu:When it is purple, it means it is beyond danger ,And when you look at the Pm 2.5 is 130 which is quite dangerous. But you look at the Pm 10 it's very, very, very dangerous. Masa: Do you see this purple a lot? Mdu: Yes, I took the device with me for like more than three months, and I was recording every week and it was bad. VO: Following the ‘purple’ danger, we head south to Sebokeng, a region persistently cloaked in layers of toxic haze, and part of the Vaal Triangle Air-shed priority area. Resident Vusi Zulu, lived close to the industrial sector for about 10 years. Vusi: There was a lot of smoke, dust. You can, even if you wash your car you can see in the morning, there's a this a a stof. VO: But even now in his new home across the valley from the factories, he still battles with asthma. Vusi: If starting raining of, the weather's changing of there's lot of smoke then I start getting the attacks. VO: Escalating the crisis and recognised as one of the most polluted places in the world is the Highveld Priority area, covering parts of Gauteng and Mpumalanga. Timothy: And that is largely due to the high concentration of coal fired power stations that we have in the area, along with coal mines and other industrial hotspots. VO: It's been the focus of a landmark constitutional challenge since 2019. Timothy: So in our Constitution, we have section 24 A of the Constitution, which is the right to an environment that is not harmful to one's health and well being. VO: Dubbed the Deadly Air Case, it was spearheaded by the Centre for Environmental Rights on behalf of Groundwork andVukani Environmental Movement and heard at the High Court in May this year. Timothy: The applicants are asking the court to force government to take further steps in the form of regulations, to reduce the levels of air pollution. VO: Contaminants from this area also find their way into the city metros. But the main PM2.5 culprits come from vehicle emissions, burning of fossil fuels and local industry, Caradee: Air Pollution will go up during winter months, when more people are burning coal and wood in Gauteng to heat water to cook food. And so you'll often see the the brown black layer of smog as you drive along the N1 VO: Dr Adeyemi gathers his data for Tshwane and its surrounds. Dr Adeyemi: During that period, there are exceedances, That means is far above the standard of South African and WHO, like in my study, I think we have about 33 days that actually exceeded, the South Africa standard VO: The difference between the South African standards for air quality and the WHO guidelines is staggering, as South Africa falls far short of the recommendations.// With Johannesburg peaking amongst the top 20 most polluted major cities in the world, July and August this year saw levels of pollution that prompted health warnings, advising some residents to "restrict activities and remain indoors" Timothy: Medical studies indicate that there is actually no safe limit when it comes to particulate matter we ideally shouldn't be exposed to at all and we shouldn't be inhaling it at all. VO: Heading off to the West Rand it gets worse, with more deadly ingredients in the mix. LINK: Prevalent in Gauteng are dust particles circulating in the air from goldmine dumps. These particles are not only toxic but contain radioactive metals. David Van Wyk: The dust contains uranium, it contains lead, it contains silica, it contains arsenic, all of them very bad poison. VO: David Van Wyk, lead researcher with the Benchmarks Foundation, is measuring the levels of radiation with a Gieger Counter, here at Tudor Shaft Informal Settlement in Krugersdorp. David Van Wyk: Normal levels of radiation is 0.10 And as we move closer to that mine dump, you will hear this device going beep beep beep faster and faster and faster. because the levels of uranium in the soil there is very high. Masa: How’s it looking now? David Van Wyk: 0.86 Masa: Oh my word so it shot up to 0.86?! And we’ve just moved a few metres David Van Wyk: It's now almost nine times higher than what is the norm for background radiation, so the area here is quite radioactive. So these people here are very close to uranium and even if you don't see any shacks on the dump itself, the wind blows the dust into the community. VO: Remnants of tailings or residue from the old mine lie unprotected here, with no warnings to keep people off the area. Cattle graze freely. For more than a decade Carte Blanche has highlighted the significance of activist Mariette Liefferink’s work. As CEO of the Federation for a Sustainable Environment she has championed the plight of communities across the goldfields of the Witwatersrand, investigating the causal links between illness and mine waste. Mariette: The research found that there is risk to human health because in this area since 1995, more than 600 persons stayed in shacks, without foundations on this dump area and adjacent to the dump area. VO: Some of these previous residents came here to meet us, community leader David Pheto, wants their stories to be heard. David: They were struggling with shortness of breath.. there's this boy, who was born in 2008, he started having a rash on his body, and it looked like skin is peeling off Jack: When it's hot I get things that look like a rash. Water comes out. Masa: So these are the marks it leaves? Jack: Yes it leaves marks that don't go away. Masa: So you say you're swollen? Siphiwe: I was always working every day, but now I can't work because of this swelling and I can't do anything that I love to do because of this swelling. VO: These accounts are anecdotal. And even though much research has been done, no epidemiological studies into the impact of radiation on the residents around South Africa's gold mines have been conducted. Mariette: The eating of the tailings by especially pregnant women and young children. exposes the inhabitants to not only the physical dangers, but also of course to transgenerational impacts because of the radioactivity. VO: However, the National Nuclear Regulator interprets its mandate narrowly, and only regulates where mining is taking place. Mariette: There are 380 radioactive mine residue areas in Gauteng, upon which approximately 400,000 people are living. VO: 270 of these facilities contain six hundred thousand tons of uranium.// And with the release of more stringent air quality guidelines by the WHO on the 22nd of September, how does South Africa even begin to meet standards that would alleviate the suffering of the hardest hit communities in pollution hotspots? Caradee: It's a tricky challenge, meeting development needs, providing services to people, while at the same time trying to curb air pollution. We've got to get to one of the interim target level guideline values from the WHO, as best as we can. VO: On request to participate in our programme, the Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development, declined to comment Timothy: We've got a very advanced set of air quality laws in place. Publishing these air quality laws and plans, that's step one; step two is actually implementing these and making sure they're enforced. Without that second step, these laws that we have, aren't worth the paper that they're written on.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): In the midst of the Covid 19 pandemic another silent killer continues to attack the people in and around Johannesburg... the deadly air that we breathe.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Take a look online at Johannesburg on IQAir's real time maps of air quality and pollution and the rankings of cities in terms of how hazardous their air is may give you a shock. Seeing Joburg up there with Indian and Chinese industrial cities is pretty scary. It is peculiar to compare the government’s SAAQIS map which uses the same data – indicators are less hazardous than the international IQAir indicators, apparently because South Africa standards are so low. Earlier this year in February the government instigated a probe into unusually high levels of sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide in Mpumalanga and Gauteng and just past, this winter has seen dangerously high levels of pollution. Johannesburg is not helped by its climate or geography. The city is surrounded by petrochemical industries and power generation industries. In winter the long weeks of static high pressure together with the heat of the concrete jungle trap the blanket of coal fired pollution for weeks on end. But the air pollution in Johannesburg, Tshwane and surrounds does not only blow in from Mpumalanga’s coal burning power stations.
metadata.Summary: In normal times poor air quality kills many people in Gauteng. In 2013, World Health Organization reported that air pollution killed almost 20,000 South Africans with the highest concentration of deadly pollution being in Tshwane and Johannesburg. These days the Covid 19 pandemic exacerbates these conditions for ill health, with the air pollution making Gauteng city dwellers more susceptible to the most acute effects of the coronavirus. It is commonly understood that air pollution kills because of respiratory disease, but sulphur dioxide in the air reacts with other substances in the air forming small deadly particles of mixed chemicals that we breathe, causing not only lung disease, but heart disease and brain disease. This is because these PM2.5 particles are so small they get carried around our bodies within oxygen to all of our organs. The South African Air Quality Information Systems (SAAQIS) recorded twice the annual average of PM2.5 pollution at the end of July this year. In early August levels of pollution exceeded the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) prompting health warnings especially in areas like Diepkloof and Jabavu advising residents to "reduce physical exertion, particularly outdoors." So we're advised to live in well-ventilated areas because of Covid but to close all our windows to keep the hazardous pollution out. What can be done to clean our skies while keeping the wheels of South Africa's economic hub turning?
metadata.Further information: Picking up from John Webb’s story in 2019 which focused on Mpumalanga – this story on air pollution and its effects in South Africa, focuses on the air pollution in and around Johannesburg and the adverse health effects it produces. Particular areas of exploration are: - How bad is the air quality in Johannesburg and the surrounding areas and why is it so? - What are the health effects attributed to air pollution? We are setting up interviews with case studies who are suffering from bad health caused by the deadly air. - Standards of data gathering and regulation in South Africa? Professor Janine Wichmann of the University of Pretoria started her own data gathering unit at AP because of the low standards of data collection in SA. We are setting up a demo of this installation with Dr Adayemi. - What are other pollutants out-with coal powered electricity generators are making an impact in Johannesburg, Tshwane and surrounds? One main pollutant prevalent in Gauteng are the radioactive dust particles discarded in old goldmine dumps. Somewhat forgotten in the mix are domestic solid fuel burning (influenced by the ‘Energy Ladder’ effect) and the Illegal burning of waste (that’s not being collected) – both particulate matter. Not to mention the fumes that exude from road vehicles (Ozone) - What actions should we be taking to tackle this issue in South Africa? Why has there been little progress in reducing air pollution? The debate about alternatives to coal power stations, ‘Nuclear vs renewable’, with the jockeying for position, is akin to the endless postponements of state corruption trials. Health and Environmental campaigners have opened the so-called Deadly Air Court Case. The applicants, under the auspices of the Centre for Environmental Rights, are arguing in the High Court that the unsafe levels of ambient air pollution be declared a violation of section 24a of The Constitution, which states that "everyone has the right to an environment not harmful to their health or wellbeing". They want the court to order the minister to introduce strict and enforceable regulations to improve air quality. Two environmental justice groups, groundWork and the Vukani Environmental Justice Movement are represented by the Centre for Environmental Rights in the case. The respondents are the president, the minister of forestry, fisheries and the environment, the national air quality officer and the MECs for agriculture and rural development in Gauteng and Mpumalanga. Heard on 17, 18 May this year, we await judgment. Further to Eskom successfully applying to postpone compliance with Minimum Emission Standards for its existing power stations in 2014, in 27 March 2020 the government posted an Amendment to the National Environmental Management Air Quality Act 39 of 2004 – NEMAQA. This ostensibly means that existing power stations do not need to comply with emission standards until 2025, provided no further amendments are passed in the meantime. WHO’s updated guidelines will be released on 22 September. The big debate within WHO is how do they apply these world guidelines in countries who are not necessarily geared to achieve these standards – then you’ve got Eskom who are one of the biggest contributors to pollution in Gauteng. In March this year Eskom said it will cost over R300 billion to upgrade its power plants to meet pollution standards. Eskom are reportedly trading off upgrading homes against its responsibility to meet air pollution standards. It installs electric stoves, gas stoves in homes, but the pollution to create the electricity and the gas is more toxic than what the stoves replace. - What are PM2.5s and why are they so relevant to this matter? In 2022 NASA are actually launching a satellite with new detectors onboard to study the distribution of these particles around the planet even further. Interviews Caradee Wright [ confirmed ] Senior Specialist Scientist: South African Medical Research Council Works in the field of air quality and finding ways to integrate public health into air quality management. Caradee also works in the broader field of environmental health, leading large epidemiological, cross-sectional community surveys to consider the impacts of environmental pollution on community health and develop appropriate interventions. Can address the WHO recommendations amongst other issues Mariette Liefferink [ confirmed ] CEO: Federation for a Sustainable Environment Will interview in situ at mine dumps in Krugersdorp. Campaigner highlighting the prevalence of radioactive dust in Joburg air.
